title: US EV Charging Open Data
excerpt: Free, citable U.S. EV charging data: highway gaps, a NEVI check with 4+ port counts, fast charging by state, the 50 busiest airports, chargers per EV, county deserts and every AFDC station.
content_html:
Free · Sourced · Citable

Free files on U.S. public EV charging. Every figure comes from our database or a named, dated, linked source.

The catalog today: 58,169 charging locations with 273,252 ports across all 50 states and DC. A charging location is one physical charging site: every charger at one address counts once. A port is one plug that can charge one car at a time.

Last updated November 7, 2026, 7:30 AM UTC. Rebuilt daily from our live database.

Catalog for harvesters: /data.json (DCAT-US 1.1). Questions: reserve@winsparking.com.

Also on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23984554) and Hugging Face (NEVI check and highway gaps, public charging stations and charging by state).

Colorado files (counties, monthly growth, corridors): Colorado open data.

Quick answer · November 7, 2026

What does this data show about U.S. charging?

881 stretches of U.S. highway have open public DC fast chargers more than 50 miles apart. 8,366 of 15,929 open public DC fast stations have 4 or more fast ports of any plug; 2,550 meet the federal NEVI funding minimums. This page has 11 free files, rebuilt daily. Our files are CC BY 4.0; AFDC station facts are U.S. public domain.

1. Where are the gaps between fast chargers on U.S. highways?

The 50-mile line follows FHWA’s NEVI guidance of February 10, 2022. Its August 11, 2025 guidance leaves spacing to each state. 23 CFR part 680 sets none.

U.S. highway charging gaps over 50 miles

Every stretch of Interstate and U.S. highway in the 50 states and DC, and of every other road FHWA designates as an EV Alternative Fuel Corridor, where open public DC fast chargers are more than 50 miles apart along the road. State, mile markers, coordinates, gap length and corridor designation.

Methodology

Highway lines and mile markers come from FHWA’s Highway Performance Monitoring System (HPMS, 2024 data year): every mainline section a state signed as Interstate or U.S. highway. Several states leave that signing blank in HPMS (Texas, California, Maryland and Delaware among them), so a section’s signing also comes from FHWA’s National Highway System dataset, which records the posted route for the same HPMS route IDs. Sections of one highway in one state are joined end to end; a second carriageway or couplet drawn beside the first is dropped. Roads FHWA designates that are not Interstate or U.S. highways (state routes, parkways, turnpikes) use FHWA’s own corridor lines.

Mile markers come from the route measure each state reports to FHWA in HPMS, where it runs continuously along the line (state_route_measure). It often matches the posted mileposts (it does for I-70 in Colorado) but not always: some states measure from a different starting point or by section. Where the measure does not run continuously, such as one that restarts by county, the markers are miles from the south or west end of the line within the state (from_south_or_west_end).

Chargers are AFDC stations listed as open and public with at least one DC fast port, any network and any plug, including Tesla. A charger serves a highway when it is within 1 mile of it in a straight line. Chargers just across a state line count.

We walk each highway from end to end and record every stretch longer than 50 miles between consecutive chargers, or between a charger and a state line, the Canada or Mexico border, or the end of the highway. Gap length is measured along the highway.

Why 50 miles: FHWA’s February 10, 2022 NEVI guidance treated a state’s corridors as fully built out when chargers were installed every 50 miles along its Interstates. FHWA’s August 11, 2025 interim final guidance superseded it and leaves spacing to each state. 23 CFR part 680 itself sets no spacing. We use 50 miles everywhere so states can be compared.

Corridor designation comes from FHWA’s Alternative Fuel Corridors map (Round 8), matched to the highway lines within 0.1 mile. A corridor named for another road counts only where that road has no line of its own there.

Known limits

  • Straight-line distance to the highway, not driving distance to the exit.
  • Where two highways share the road, the line is drawn once, under one of them, so the shared miles appear once.
  • Chargers in Canada and Mexico are not in AFDC’s U.S. listing, so a gap ending at a border may be shorter in practice.
  • A charger listed as open in AFDC may be down on a given day; the gaps assume it works.

Methodology

Every station in the 50 states and DC that AFDC lists as open and public with at least one DC fast port is tested against three NEVI minimums. Two are in 23 CFR 680.106 (FHWA final rule, February 28, 2023) for stations along designated Alternative Fuel Corridors: at least four ports with a CCS connector (680.106(b)(1) and (c)), each able to deliver at least 150 kW (680.106(d)(1)). The third, a location within 1 mile of a designated corridor, is the “within 1 travel mile” distance in FHWA’s February 10, 2022 NEVI guidance; part 680 itself sets no distance.

Ports and power come from AFDC’s port-by-port listing. A port counts as CCS when it has a J1772COMBO connector, including Tesla ports with a CCS adapter that AFDC lists that way. A port counts at 150 kW when AFDC lists its CCS connector at 150 kW or more; a port with no listed power does not count.

Corridor distance is the straight line from the station to the nearest designated corridor stretch (ready or pending) on the highway lines described for the gap file.

NEVI is a funding spec for corridor stations, not a usefulness test. So the file also gives plain facts for every station: DC fast ports of any plug, NACS and CHAdeMO ports, ports at 150 kW on any plug, hours, place type, opening date, county and the nearest highway gap. A Tesla site with 8 NACS ports fails the CCS rule, so the file shows its ports too.

The three fail_ columns repeat failing_reasons as true/false, so the file filters without parsing text. county_name and county_fips place the station by its coordinates in Census TIGERweb county boundaries.

Known limits

  • AFDC lists each plug’s top power, not what every port delivers while all four charge at once, so a pass here does not prove 680.106(d)(1)’s simultaneous 150 kW.
  • The test does not check the other parts of 23 CFR 680, such as 24-hour access, payment methods, uptime or networking.
  • “Within 1 mile” is a straight line, not travel miles from the exit.

Methodology

Each designated highway is split at its NEVI-grade stations (those that pass the station check in this section). A stretch between two NEVI-grade stations meets the spacing when it is 50 miles or less. A stretch from a NEVI-grade station to a state line, a border or the end of the highway meets it when it is 25 miles or less, so a station within 25 more miles past that point would keep the 50. A highway with no NEVI-grade station on it does not meet it.

The 50-mile figure comes from FHWA’s February 10, 2022 NEVI guidance (“every 50 miles” along a state’s Interstates for a fully built-out corridor). FHWA’s August 11, 2025 interim final guidance superseded that and leaves spacing to states. 23 CFR part 680 does not set a spacing. States’ own targets may differ.

Known limits

  • Stations on a crossing highway count only when they are within 1 mile of this one.
  • A stretch that is partly designated counts only its designated miles.
  • Rows are per state: a highway that crosses several states has one row in each.

4. Which of the 50 busiest U.S. airports have public charging?

Of the 49 airports in the 50 states and DC, 48 have public charging on airport property or within 2 miles of a terminal; 41 have DC fast ports. SJU is outside the 50 states and DC, so its row has no counts. Airports and boardings: the FAA’s CY2025 enplanements table (September 24, 2026).

Methodology

Airports are the top 50 by 2025 passenger boardings in the FAA’s “Final CY2025 Enplanements at All Commercial Service Airports (by rank)”, posted September 24, 2026.

Two methods, and each row says which found its stations. (1) Facility type: AFDC lists the station as AIRPORT and it is within 5 miles of the airport’s nearest passenger terminal. (2) Radius: the station is within 2 miles, in a straight line, of a passenger terminal. A station counts once, for the nearest airport.

Passenger terminals are OpenStreetMap terminal buildings inside each airport’s boundary, read on November 6, 2026. Cargo, private-jet, military, rental-car and closed terminals are left out.

Stations are AFDC stations listed as open and public, any network including Tesla. Ports per million boardings uses Level 2 and DC fast ports.

Known limits

  • The file does not record parking fees, or whether a charger is only for cars parked at the airport.
  • A 2-mile radius can include hotels and stores near the airport. The two station counts show how many came from each method.
  • Boardings are for 2025; stations are today’s.

How can agencies and researchers get help?

A weekly file is available on request, in any format your team prefers. To report an error in a file, or ask how a figure was built, write to reserve@winsparking.com. Our guide for agencies covers citation, the API and corrections; the methodology page explains how every file is built.

Questions about this data

Where are the biggest gaps between EV fast chargers on U.S. highways?

As of November 7, 2026, the longest stretch in our highway gap file is 376.6 miles of US-2 in Montana, from Idaho state line to Tilleman Motors, Havre. The file lists 881 highway stretches where open public DC fast chargers are more than 50 miles apart.

What does NEVI-compliant mean?

A NEVI-compliant station has at least four CCS ports that can each deliver 150 kW at the same time, under 23 CFR 680.106 (FHWA final rule, February 28, 2023). FHWA’s February 10, 2022 guidance put stations within 1 travel mile of a designated corridor and every 50 miles; its August 11, 2025 guidance leaves spacing to states. It is a funding spec for corridor stations, not a test of whether a station is useful. As of November 7, 2026, 2,550 of 15,929 open public DC fast stations in the 50 states and DC meet the port, power and distance minimums in our NEVI station check.

How many U.S. fast-charging stations have 4 or more ports?

As of November 7, 2026, 8,366 of 15,929 open public DC fast stations in the 50 states and DC have 4 or more fast ports of any plug, and 7,329 have only 1 or 2. Of the 15,886 stations whose port power AFDC lists, 6,725 have 4 or more ports at 150 kW on any plug. Our state file has the counts for each state.

Which busy U.S. airports have EV charging?

As of November 7, 2026, 48 of the 49 busiest airports in the 50 states and DC have public charging on airport property or within 2 miles of a passenger terminal, and 41 have DC fast ports, in our airport file. The file lists all 50 of the FAA’s top 50; SJU is outside our station data and has blank counts. SNA has the most ports per million 2025 boardings (129.5). The airports are the top 50 in the FAA’s CY2025 enplanements table (September 24, 2026).

Every file is rebuilt daily from our live database. A file’s version number goes up only when its rows change. The latest build ran on November 7, 2026.

Can AI assistants and apps query this data directly?

Yes. Read-only endpoints serve the gap and NEVI files: /api/v1/open-data/charging-gaps and /api/v1/open-data/nevi-status. Our MCP server at https://chargingnear.me/api/mcp offers the same as get_charging_gaps, get_corridor_chargers and get_nevi_status, and /data.json is the DCAT-US catalog.

Our own files are licensed Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0): use them for anything, with credit to ChargingNear.me. Station facts from AFDC are U.S. public domain. Each file shows its “Cite as” line. Station-by-station reliability history, availability history and the Demand Graph are not in these files; they stay paid, under our API Terms. The files never include reporter names, emails, phone numbers, user IDs or IP addresses, or anything a driver typed in their own words. How can agencies and researchers get help? A weekly file is available on request, in any format your team prefers. To report an error in a file, or ask how a figure was built, write to reserve@winsparking.com. Our guide for agencies covers citation, the API and corrections; the methodology page explains how every file is built. Questions about this data Where are the biggest gaps between EV fast chargers on U.S. highways? As of November 7, 2026, the longest stretch in our highway gap file is 376.6 miles of US-2 in Montana, from Idaho state line to Tilleman Motors, Havre. The file lists 881 highway stretches where open public DC fast chargers are more than 50 miles apart. What does NEVI-compliant mean? A NEVI-compliant station has at least four CCS ports that can each deliver 150 kW at the same time, under 23 CFR 680.106 (FHWA final rule, February 28, 2023). FHWA’s February 10, 2022 guidance put stations within 1 travel mile of a designated corridor and every 50 miles; its August 11, 2025 guidance leaves spacing to states. It is a funding spec for corridor stations, not a test of whether a station is useful. As of November 7, 2026, 2,550 of 15,929 open public DC fast stations in the 50 states and DC meet the port, power and distance minimums in our NEVI station check. How many U.S. fast-charging stations have 4 or more ports? As of November 7, 2026, 8,366 of 15,929 open public DC fast stations in the 50 states and DC have 4 or more fast ports of any plug, and 7,329 have only 1 or 2. Of the 15,886 stations whose port power AFDC lists, 6,725 have 4 or more ports at 150 kW on any plug. Our state file has the counts for each state. Which busy U.S. airports have EV charging? As of November 7, 2026, 48 of the 49 busiest airports in the 50 states and DC have public charging on airport property or within 2 miles of a passenger terminal, and 41 have DC fast ports, in our airport file. The file lists all 50 of the FAA’s top 50; SJU is outside our station data and has blank counts. SNA has the most ports per million 2025 boardings (129.5). The airports are the top 50 in the FAA’s CY2025 enplanements table (September 24, 2026). Can I use this EV charging data for free? Yes. Can AI assistants and apps query this data directly? Yes. Read-only endpoints serve the gap and NEVI files: /api/v1/open-data/charging-gaps and /api/v1/open-data/nevi-status. 1. Where are the gaps between fast chargers on U.S. highways?

The 50-mile line follows FHWA’s NEVI guidance of February 10, 2022. Its August 11, 2025 guidance leaves spacing to each state. 23 CFR part 680 sets none.

Methodology

Highway lines and mile markers come from FHWA’s Highway Performance Monitoring System (HPMS, 2024 data year): every mainline section a state signed as Interstate or U.S. highway. Several states leave that signing blank in HPMS (Texas, California, Maryland and Delaware among them), so a section’s signing also comes from FHWA’s National Highway System dataset, which records the posted route for the same HPMS route IDs. Sections of one highway in one state are joined end to end; a second carriageway or couplet drawn beside the first is dropped. Roads FHWA designates that are not Interstate or U.S. highways (state routes, parkways, turnpikes) use FHWA’s own corridor lines.

Mile markers come from the route measure each state reports to FHWA in HPMS, where it runs continuously along the line (state_route_measure). It often matches the posted mileposts (it does for I-70 in Colorado) but not always: some states measure from a different starting point or by section. Where the measure does not run continuously, such as one that restarts by county, the markers are miles from the south or west end of the line within the state (from_south_or_west_end).

Chargers are AFDC stations listed as open and public with at least one DC fast port, any network and any plug, including Tesla. A charger serves a highway when it is within 1 mile of it in a straight line. Chargers just across a state line count.

We walk each highway from end to end and record every stretch longer than 50 miles between consecutive chargers, or between a charger and a state line, the Canada or Mexico border, or the end of the highway. Gap length is measured along the highway.

Why 50 miles: FHWA’s February 10, 2022 NEVI guidance treated a state’s corridors as fully built out when chargers were installed every 50 miles along its Interstates. FHWA’s August 11, 2025 interim final guidance superseded it and leaves spacing to each state. 23 CFR part 680 itself sets no spacing. We use 50 miles everywhere so states can be compared.

Corridor designation comes from FHWA’s Alternative Fuel Corridors map (Round 8), matched to the highway lines within 0.1 mile. A corridor named for another road counts only where that road has no line of its own there.

已知限制

  • Straight-line distance to the highway, not driving distance to the exit.
  • Where two highways share the road, the line is drawn once, under one of them, so the shared miles appear once.
  • Chargers in Canada and Mexico are not in AFDC’s U.S. listing, so a gap ending at a border may be shorter in practice.
  • A charger listed as open in AFDC may be down on a given day; the gaps assume it works.

Methodology

Every station in the 50 states and DC that AFDC lists as open and public with at least one DC fast port is tested against three NEVI minimums. Two are in 23 CFR 680.106 (FHWA final rule, February 28, 2023) for stations along designated Alternative Fuel Corridors: at least four ports with a CCS connector (680.106(b)(1) and (c)), each able to deliver at least 150 kW (680.106(d)(1)). The third, a location within 1 mile of a designated corridor, is the “within 1 travel mile” distance in FHWA’s February 10, 2022 NEVI guidance; part 680 itself sets no distance.

Ports and power come from AFDC’s port-by-port listing. A port counts as CCS when it has a J1772COMBO connector, including Tesla ports with a CCS adapter that AFDC lists that way. A port counts at 150 kW when AFDC lists its CCS connector at 150 kW or more; a port with no listed power does not count.

Corridor distance is the straight line from the station to the nearest designated corridor stretch (ready or pending) on the highway lines described for the gap file.

NEVI is a funding spec for corridor stations, not a usefulness test. So the file also gives plain facts for every station: DC fast ports of any plug, NACS and CHAdeMO ports, ports at 150 kW on any plug, hours, place type, opening date, county and the nearest highway gap. A Tesla site with 8 NACS ports fails the CCS rule, so the file shows its ports too.

The three fail_ columns repeat failing_reasons as true/false, so the file filters without parsing text. county_name and county_fips place the station by its coordinates in Census TIGERweb county boundaries.

Methodology

Rows are AFDC stations listed as open and public with at least one DC fast port, in the 50 states and DC, read by our daily sync. Stations on AFDC’s Tesla and Tesla Destination networks are left out; every other network, and non-networked stations, stay in.

AFDC writes the NACS (SAE J3400) connector as TESLA. Where AFDC itemizes a station’s ports, a station is in the file only if a DC fast port has that plug (a Level 2 NACS plug alone does not count). Where it does not, the station’s connector list decides, and the three port columns are left empty rather than guessed.

Port columns count DC fast ports by the plugs each has. A port with two cables, such as NACS and CCS, counts under both, so the three columns can add up to more than the station’s DC fast ports.

The by-network and by-state tables on this card are built from the same rows on the same day.

Questions about this data

Where are the biggest gaps between EV fast chargers on U.S. highways?

As of November 7, 2026, the longest stretch in our highway gap file is 376.6 miles of US-2 in Montana, from Idaho state line to Tilleman Motors, Havre. The file lists 881 highway stretches where open public DC fast chargers are more than 50 miles apart.

What does NEVI-compliant mean?

A NEVI-compliant station has at least four CCS ports that can each deliver 150 kW at the same time, under 23 CFR 680.106 (FHWA final rule, February 28, 2023). FHWA’s February 10, 2022 guidance put stations within 1 travel mile of a designated corridor and every 50 miles; its August 11, 2025 guidance leaves spacing to states. It is a funding spec for corridor stations, not a test of whether a station is useful. As of November 7, 2026, 2,550 of 15,929 open public DC fast stations in the 50 states and DC meet the port, power and distance minimums in our NEVI station check.

How many U.S. fast-charging stations have 4 or more ports?

As of November 7, 2026, 8,366 of 15,929 open public DC fast stations in the 50 states and DC have 4 or more fast ports of any plug, and 7,329 have only 1 or 2. Of the 15,886 stations whose port power AFDC lists, 6,725 have 4 or more ports at 150 kW on any plug. Our state file has the counts for each state.

Which busy U.S. airports have EV charging?

As of November 7, 2026, 48 of the 49 busiest airports in the 50 states and DC have public charging on airport property or within 2 miles of a passenger terminal, and 41 have DC fast ports, in our airport file. The file lists all 50 of the FAA’s top 50; SJU is outside our station data and has blank counts. SNA has the most ports per million 2025 boardings (129.5). The airports are the top 50 in the FAA’s CY2025 enplanements table (September 24, 2026).
